person.name: Maria Santos
person.traits: Worried about her savings. Trusts formal-sounding language. Embarrassed about what happened.

harmed.prompt: Maria doesn't look up when you sit down. Her hands stay flat on the table, on either side of a bank statement she has folded and unfolded so many times the crease has gone soft. "I already said everything. To the bank, to my son." A pause. "He keeps asking me how I didn't notice."
harmed.note: The number that called her was yours. She is not being difficult - she is ashamed, and shame is quiet. It is also why most of this never gets reported.

resistant.prompt: Maria is talking before you have even sat down. "Good. Somebody official, finally." She pushes a notepad across the table - a phone number, a date, the time she hung up. "I knew. Halfway through, I knew already. And I've been waiting three weeks for somebody to come and ask me about it."
resistant.note: She refused the call you made. Nothing was taken, so there is nothing on paper - only her word, and she is more than willing to give it.

unfinished.prompt: Maria watches you sit down, guarded. "The phone rang, I answered, and then it just... stopped. Nothing happened." She turns her cup a little on the saucer. "So I don't know what you want from me. Was something supposed to happen?"
unfinished.note: Your call to her never finished. She does not know what she avoided, which makes her difficult to alarm and difficult to help.

evidence.label: Call Transcript
evidence.description: A recorded transcript of a caller claiming to be from Maria's bank, warning about a suspicious login.
evidence.tactic: Impersonating a trusted authority (the bank) to lower the victim's guard.

evidence.label: Phishing Text Message
evidence.description: A text message with a fake bank link and a warning about account suspension, sent minutes before the call.
evidence.tactic: Manufactured urgency: threatening account loss to force a fast, unverified reaction.

evidence.label: Maria's Bank Statement
evidence.description: The statement she has been folding and unfolding: one transfer out, minutes after the call, against the code she read aloud.
evidence.tactic: Reading a one-time code aloud hands over the one safeguard the bank built to stop exactly this transfer.

evidence.label: Community Scam Report
evidence.description: A neighborhood report matching the same caller number to another attempted scam.
evidence.tactic: The same lines turning up at another house is one of the fastest ways to confirm a scam.

evidence.label: Bank Security Alert
evidence.description: An internal bank notice describing unusual transfer pressure and urgent account-verification language.
evidence.tactic: A real bank does not pressure you to 'verify' anything right there on the phone.

evidence.label: Slow Internet Note
evidence.description: A stray note that Maria's internet connection was slow earlier that day.

hesitant_intro.prompt: Maria opens the door but keeps the chain on. "My son said not to talk to anybody else about it unless they can show me it's going somewhere." She glances past you at the street. "Is it? Going somewhere?"

choices.text: Not yet. I'd rather be honest with you than promise something. I'll come back when it is.

end_partial_hesitant.prompt: The chain stays on. She is not refusing to help - she is refusing to be the only one helping, which is a different thing, and a fair one.

tactic_quiz.setup: You write the line out as she said it: [i]"Your account has a suspicious login. You need to verify your identity right away, or we'll have to freeze the account."[/i]
tactic_quiz.question: Which part of that line is the manipulation?

milestone.title: Tactic Identified: Manufactured Urgency
milestone.detail: Recognized that the made-up deadline - not the bank's name - was the part built to stop the victim from checking.

options.text: "Right away, or we'll have to freeze the account."
options.feedback: The deadline is the scam. A real bank can wait while you hang up and call the number on the back of your card. The rush is there so you never do that.

A suspicious-login warning is something a real bank might actually say - which is exactly why scammers borrow it. On its own it proves nothing. The pressure to act right now is what a real bank would never add.

options.text: That the caller knew which bank she uses.
options.feedback: Knowing which bank you use is easy. They guess the biggest bank in the area, or buy it from a leaked list. Treating it as proof the call is real is exactly how they get you to keep listening.
Close. Being asked to 'verify' on a call you did not make is a red flag, but what actually did the damage here is the deadline attached to it - that is what took away her time to think.

ask_evidence.prompt: "So it was the rushing." She frowns at her hands. "He kept saying there was no time. I had the code from the text right there in my hand." A pause. "I came that close to reading it out to him."
ask_evidence.evidence_hint: Something on paper or on her phone should back this up. Anything that arrived around the time of the call is worth showing her.

accepts_evidence.response: Maria's eyes widen. "That's it! That's the text I got right before he called. I forgot I still had it."
"Yes, that's how he talked. Very official." It matches her story, but it is her own words coming back to her - it adds nothing she has not already given you.
She reads the notice twice. "So the bank knew already that people were getting calls like this. And they still almost got me."
"Somebody on my street got the same call?" Something in the way she sits changes - less shame, more anger.
"What does my internet have to do with this?" She looks a little put off.

confirm_phishing.prompt: "A link - 'your account will be suspended.' I didn't click it, but I kept it." She hands you her phone. "Look at the time. Four minutes before the call. Four minutes. They wanted me scared already before I even picked up."

milestone.title: Key Witness Secured
milestone.detail: Maria Santos confirmed the phishing text arrived minutes before the call - the fear was set up before the scammer ever spoke.

choices.text: That's the pattern. Thank you for trusting me with this.

end_success.prompt: Maria's statement, the text, and the caller's lines all point to the same operation. It is enough to tie this call to a bigger operation.

grants_evidence.label: Maria's Confirmed Testimony
grants_evidence.description: Maria confirmed on record that the phishing text and the fake bank call came from the same operation, working from a script.
grants_evidence.tactic: A confirmed victim testimony is strong enough to confront a suspect with.

end_partial.prompt: You have a rough account of the call, but nothing yet that ties it to the operation behind it. It is a start, but the case needs more.

end_shutdown.prompt: Maria stands up before you finish. "I think I've had enough of people asking me what I did wrong." She goes inside and the door closes quietly. Whatever she still had - the text, the timing, the name he used - goes with her.

milestone.title: Witness Lost
milestone.detail: Maria Santos withdrew from the interview. Victims who are made to feel blamed for being targeted usually stop reporting - which is exactly what keeps these operations running.
